name: Brain Computer Interfaces
title: Brain Computer Interfaces
answer: Brain computer interfaces are systems that read signals directly from the brain and translate them into commands for external devices or software. In medical AI, the scope includes assistive communication for people with paralysis, motor rehabilitation after stroke or spinal cord injury, and monitoring of neurological conditions such as epilepsy or depression. The field sits between neurophysiology, signal processing, and machine learning, and it covers both invasive implants and noninvasive headsets. This site tracks these systems alongside its catalogue of 1000 medical AI models and 803 scientific models.

sections.body: Brain computer interfaces are systems that read signals directly from the brain and translate them into commands for external devices or software. In medical AI, the scope includes assistive communication for people with paralysis, motor rehabilitation after stroke or spinal cord injury, and monitoring of neurological conditions such as epilepsy or depression. The field sits between neurophysiology, signal processing, and machine learning, and it covers both invasive implants and noninvasive headsets. This site tracks these systems alongside its catalogue of 1000 medical AI models and 803 scientific models.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Invasive brain computer interfaces rely on implanted electrode arrays or cortical strips connected to small processing units, often with wireless telemetry to external computers. Noninvasive systems use electroencephalography caps, functional near infrared spectroscopy, or magnetoencephalography, with signals digitized and streamed to local workstations or cloud services. The computational load is modest for basic cursor control but grows for real time decoding of speech or limb movement, so many labs use dedicated GPUs and low latency data pipelines. Clinical deployments require hospital grade device management, secure data storage, and integration with electronic health records.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The typical pipeline begins with recording neural activity during a task or imagined movement, then cleaning the signal to remove muscle and electrical noise. Features such as spike rates, local field potentials, or spectral power are extracted and fed into a decoder, often a recurrent network, a convolutional network, or a state space model, that maps brain patterns to intended actions. The decoder is trained on labeled examples from the user, then updated periodically as the brain adapts, a process called co adaptation. Validation uses held out sessions and closed loop tasks like moving a cursor to a target or selecting letters on a screen.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Brain computer interfaces raise distinct privacy and consent issues because they collect intimate neural data that can reveal mood, fatigue, or hidden attitudes. Implanted devices carry surgical risk, infection risk, and long term stability concerns, while noninvasive devices face questions about data ownership and third party access. Regulatory oversight generally falls under medical device rules for implants and clinical software, with separate rules for research use. The site tracks active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, and brain computer interface makers face similar exposure if a device fails or a decoder produces a harmful command. Provenance of training data matters because decoders trained on one person rarely transfer cleanly to another, so consent, data lineage, and model versioning are essential.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The near term focus is on reliable communication for people with severe motor impairment, with typing speeds and speech decoding improving but still below natural conversation. Longer term work aims at restoring movement through spinal or peripheral stimulation, treating neuropsychiatric conditions with closed loop neuromodulation, and merging brain computer interfaces with general AI assistants for context aware control. Wider use will depend on reducing calibration time, improving wireless implants, and building standards for neural data protection. The field is likely to remain a specialized medical and research area for years before any consumer use becomes routine.
